title: Signals [kill]
description:
## kill
`kill` sends a signal to a process. Despite the name, it doesn't always kill - it sends any signal you choose.

```bash
kill <pid>          # sends SIGTERM (polite: please stop)
kill -9 <pid>       # sends SIGKILL (forced: stop NOW)
kill -STOP <pid>    # sends SIGSTOP (pause)
kill -CONT <pid>    # sends SIGCONT (resume)
```

### Common signals:
| Signal | Number | Meaning |
|--------|--------|---------|
| SIGTERM | 15 | Terminate (can be caught) |
| SIGKILL | 9 | Kill (cannot be caught) |
| SIGSTOP | 19 | Pause (cannot be caught) |
| SIGCONT | 18 | Resume |
| SIGINT | 2 | Interrupt (Ctrl+C) |

### Finding processes:
```bash
ps aux              # list all processes
ps aux | grep name  # find a specific process
```

### SIGTERM vs SIGKILL:
- `SIGTERM` asks nicely. The program can clean up (save files, close connections) before exiting.
- `SIGKILL` forces it. No cleanup. Use only when SIGTERM doesn't work.

Always try `kill <pid>` first. Only use `kill -9` as a last resort.
